transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-28
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Catalyst - Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (Catalyst - CTO), Sofia Kim (Catalyst - DevOps)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/sandbox-invite, https://redwood.ai/security-pack, docs://sdk-quickstart (note: internal)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick SDK walkthrough for Catalyst Systems focused on Python and TypeScript quickstarts, environment variables and auth patterns, CI/CD secrets, and options for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment. Agreed to spin up sandbox, run latency/cost pilot, and share security docs. Next steps and owners at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh we're gonna run through the SDK quickstart for both Python and TypeScript, cover auth patterns, and then leave time for questions. Is that still the plan on your side?
[00:07] Marta Ruiz: Yep that's perfect. We're mostly trying to validate auth flow and how we can slot Redwood into our microservices. Also curious about env and CI secrets patterns.
[00:15] Priya Nair: Awesome. Quick note, I'll jump into the code snippets and run the live quickstart in the sandbox account we provisioned. Jordan will cover pricing and deployment options.
[00:22] Liam O'Connor: Cool, and just to set expectations, our latency SLO is 150 ms p95 for user-facing completions, and we currently want to compare hosted vs Dedicated.
[00:30] Priya Nair: Got it. We'll show both. The SDK exposes a simple client: in Python it's from redwood import Client then client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')). For TS it's import { Redwood } from '@redwoodai/sdk' and new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }).
[00:49] Sofia Kim: Quick question — do you support short-lived keys for CI runners? We don't want long lived tokens checked into GitHub.
[00:55] Jordan Lee: Yes, we recommend ephemeral keys for CI, you can mint short-lived tokens via the Console or via our API. Typical pattern is store KMS-wrapped secret in GitHub Actions and retrieve at workflow start. We'll share an example workflow.
[01:12] Priya Nair: I'm going to paste the Python quickstart in chat and run a small completion. Heads up transcription might garble some names. (typing)
[01:25] [TYPE OUT LOUD] Python snippet: import os
from redwood import Client
client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate('Write a short product blurb for Catalyst Systems')
print(resp.text)
[01:45] Marta Ruiz: Looks straightforward. When you say client.generate, is that hitting hosted Redwood API or do we set region/endpoint for private deployments?
[01:52] Priya Nair: By default it points at hosted api.redwood.ai. You can override base_url in the client constructor: Client(api_key=..., base_url='https://private.catalyst.redwood.local') for private or a VPC edge endpoint. Jordan can talk about routing and regioning.
[02:06] Jordan Lee: For Dedicated or Private you get a vanity endpoint and we support VPC peering or private link. The other option is to use our regional hosted endpoints to reduce egress latency.
[02:18] Liam O'Connor: And how do you handle RBAC within the Console? We need to give devs limited access and keep auditing.
[02:24] Jordan Lee: Console supports SSO SAML/SCIM, role-based access controls, and audit logs. All admin actions are logged and can be exported. Also integrates with customer KMS for key wrapping.
[02:36] Sofia Kim: Do you retain requests? We have strict data retention rules.
[02:39] Jordan Lee: You can choose retention policies per project. Hosted defaults to 30 days but enterprise customers often opt for zero retention and send logs to customer-managed storage. We'll include the exact fields in the security pack.
[02:50] Priya Nair: Back to code — in TypeScript the example is const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const resp = await client.chat.create({ messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Summarize the last meeting' }] })
console.log(resp.output[0].content)
[03:10] Marta Ruiz: That response shape, is it stable across SDK versions? We need contract stability for our app teams.
[03:15] Priya Nair: We keep backward compatible shapes but do support pinned model versions and client versions. You can lock to a specific SDK version in package.json and pin model versions in the route config.
[03:28] Liam O'Connor: For benchmarking, what's the best way to run perf tests? We want to approximate our real user patterns.
[03:33] Priya Nair: We recommend replaying production prompts through our bench harness — we can provide a runner, or you can hit the sandbox endpoints with your production-like load. For p95 latency we recommend dedicated pools with predictable throughput.
[03:48] Marta Ruiz: Any gotchas on batching and streaming we should watch for?
[03:52] Priya Nair: Streaming reduces latency for first token but complicates batching; the client supports both. If you need high throughput and low tail latency, consider prefix caching and durable KV cache if you have repeated prompts. Note: KV cache sometimes transcribed as KV cash in past calls.
[04:09] Sofia Kim: What about quantization or model variants for cost control?
[04:12] Jordan Lee: Redwood Optimize will suggest quantized variants and batching configurations. For example, q4_0b models lower token cost but may slightly affect quality — we can run evals on your prompts.
[04:25] Liam O'Connor: Regarding networking — our infra team requires private endpoints for production. How long does Private deployment take to stand up?
[04:32] Jordan Lee: Private deployments typically take 4-6 weeks depending on network approvals. Dedicated is faster, often 2-3 weeks post-contract. We can do a pilot in hosted while the private provisioning completes.
[04:44] Marta Ruiz: Can you show the .env and GitHub Actions example now?
[04:47] Priya Nair: Sure. .env local dev: REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-•••••
GitHub Actions snippet:
- name: Checkout
  uses: actions/checkout@v3
- name: Inject secrets
  run: echo "REDWOOD_API_KEY=${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
- name: Run tests
  run: pytest --maxfail=1 --disable-warnings
We recommend using ephemeral CI tokens and rotate them. We'll paste a complete gist.
[05:20] Marta Ruiz: Nice. One of our concerns is cost visibility — how do we track token costs per route?
[05:25] Jordan Lee: Console provides token-level breakdowns per route and per API key, and you can tag traffic. For Dedicated you get more granular breakdowns and you can enforce quotas by route.
[05:35] Liam O'Connor: Competitor question — have others done anything similar? Are you able to run if we wanted to compare with OpenAI endpoints?
[05:42] Jordan Lee: Yes, you can run head-to-head benchmarks using the same prompt sets. We've done comparisons with OpenAI and Anthropic, and we can share example spreadsheets. Note differences in pricing model and network egress.
[05:55] Priya Nair: I'm going to run a quick live test in the sandbox, just a simple chat completion. (types)
[06:02] [Sandbox log] Request sent to sandbox.redwood.ai — response ~120ms
[06:06] Priya Nair: Response came back ~120 ms p95 for that small prompt in the sandbox region, but your production variance will differ.
[06:15] Marta Ruiz: That's encouraging. For PII we have to mask at edge — do you have client-side redaction patterns?
[06:21] Jordan Lee: We do support client-side redaction libraries and server-side transformations. You can run a pre-processing step in your app or use our routing hooks to apply transforms.
[06:32] Sofia Kim: Any limitations with our current stack (Kubernetes + Istio)?
[06:36] Priya Nair: No major issues. For Private deployments we install an edge component that is Istio-friendly; we also have Helm charts. We'll share ops docs.
[06:47] Liam O'Connor: For compliance, what docs will you send?
[06:50] Jordan Lee: We'll send SOC 2 Type II docs, ISO-27001 summary, and our encryption architecture. Also include sample SLA and data processing addendum.
[07:02] Marta Ruiz: Cool. One operational question: if we pin to a model and there's a critical vulnerability or regression, what's the rollback path?
[07:09] Priya Nair: We expose rollout controls in Console — canary percentages and automatic fallback to previous model variant. For Dedicated you can request emergency rollback and we coordinate via support.
[07:20] Jordan Lee: Let's talk about next steps. We'll provision a sandbox project for you, share the security pack, and set up a benchmarking session. Marta, can you share the example repo and latency targets?
[07:30] Marta Ruiz: Yes I'll send the repo link and a spreadsheet with sample prompts by Monday.
[07:36] Jordan Lee: Great. Any final questions?
[07:39] Liam O'Connor: One small thing — what's the expected cost delta for dedicated pools vs hosted on a per-100k token basis?
[07:46] Jordan Lee: It depends on usage patterns but dedicated becomes cost-effective above certain sustained throughput; we'll run numbers in the pricing sheet we'll send. Expect order-of-magnitude differences based on batching and quantization choices.
[07:58] Priya Nair: Ok wrapping up, I'll paste the GitHub Actions gist and the sandbox invite link in the follow up email.
[08:05] Jordan Lee: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the action items. Note — some words in this transcript may be mis-heard.
